RTM.title: Regional Transit Measure
RTM.question: To prevent major service cuts to BART and other transit, avoid increased traffic, and reduce pollution by: Preserving BART, Caltrain, VTA, SamTrans, AC Transit, Muni, other transit for everyone, including workers, students, seniors, persons with disabilities; Supporting transit safety, cleanliness, affordability, reliability; Repairing targeted roads/potholes; Requiring financial transparency, oversight, accountability; shall the measure enacting a 0.5% (Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo, Santa Clara counties), and 1% (San Francisco) sales tax for 14 years generating approximately $980,000,000 annually, be adopted?
RTM.threshold: 50%+1 of all votes cast in the five Bay Area counties
RTM.analysis: This measure was placed on the ballot by voter initiative, signed by the requisite number of voters within the Public Transit Revenue Measure District (“District”). The District was created by the Legislature through Senate Bill 63 (“SB 63”) in 2025 (Government Code sections 67700-67788), which was enacted to preserve and improve public transit service in the San Francisco Bay Area. The District comprises the counties of Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo, and Santa Clara, and the City and County of San Francisco, and is governed by the same board that governs the Metropolitan Transportation Commission (“MTC”). SB 63 authorizes District voters to approve a retail transactions and use tax (commonly referred to as a sales tax) for specified purposes. This measure would impose a tax of 0.5% in the counties of Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo, and Santa Clara and 1.0% in the City and County of San Francisco. The tax would be imposed and collected in largely the same manner as a state-imposed sales tax. The tax would be in effect for 14 years and would not count toward the statutory limit on combined local sales tax rates. It is estimated that the tax would raise approximately $980 million per year. After payment of defined costs, including election costs and administrative expenses, the District must transfer all remaining revenues to MTC and county transportation agencies for distribution and expenditure according to percentages set forth in the measure, which vary by county and recipient. Recipients include BART, Muni, Caltrain, AC Transit, Santa Clara Valley Transportation Authority, San Francisco Bay Ferry, Golden Gate Transit, smaller bus operators in Alameda and Contra Costa Counties, and county transportation agencies. Revenues would also support free and reduced-cost transit transfers, expansion of the Clipper START reduced-fare program, accessibility programs, mapping and wayfinding and transit priority projects and programs, and repavement projects for roads served by fixed-route transit. While the tax would be imposed throughout the District, the allocation of revenue generated in each county, and the authorized uses of those funds, would vary. For example, 64.70% of all revenues generated in Alameda County would be allocated to BART for transit operations expenses. By contrast, 84.37% of all revenues generated in Santa Clara County would be allocated to the Santa Clara Valley Transportation Authority for public transit expenses and roadway repavement projects on roads served by fixed-route transit. Such repavement projects would be an authorized use of measure revenues in Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo, and Santa Clara counties, but would not be authorized in the City and County of San Francisco. Revenue allocation is set forth in Section 12 of the measure. Tax revenues would be subject to accountability requirements in SB 63, which requires BART, Muni, AC Transit, and Caltrain to undergo financial efficiency reviews and adopt implementation plans and authorizes MTC to withhold funds from any of those operators for noncompliance. The measure would also require an independent oversight committee to review whether all revenues are distributed as required. The tax would become effective if approved by a majority of those voting on the measure throughout the entire District.
RTM.yes_means: a vote to impose the tax described above for 14 years.
RTM.no_means: a vote against imposing the tax.
RTM.how_placed: On May 26, 2026, the “Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative” was submitted to election officials in Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo, and Santa Clara counties, as well as the City and County of San Francisco. The petition included 306,288 unverified signatures. State law required 187,119 valid signatures to qualify the initiative for the ballot. This number is equal to 5% of the total number of registered voters within the District. A random check of the signatures submitted by the proponents of the initiative petition showed that an estimated 235,503 signatures were valid. Because this number was greater than the 205,831 signature threshold, which represents 110% of the required number of signatures, the petition was found to be sufficient. On July 1, 2026, the District Elections Official certified that the petition contained enough valid signatures to qualify for the November 3, 2026 ballot.

A.title: Charter Changes Affecting Various City Departments and Commissions
A.question: Shall the City amend the Charter to align it with how some City departments currently operate, change some processes, eliminate or reorganize certain commissions and advisory bodies, and require the Board of Supervisors to amend voter-approved laws to enact some of these changes?
A.way_it_is_now: The Charter is the City’s constitution and establishes the organization, powers, and responsibilities for many City departments. The Charter and other voter-approved laws also create many City commissions and advisory bodies and describe their powers, duties, membership and removal rules, and reporting requirements. Over time, some of these laws have become obsolete. The Charter and most laws passed by the voters can only be changed with voter approval.
A.proposal:
Proposition A would align the Charter with how some City departments currently operate, change some processes, and eliminate or reorganize certain commissions and advisory bodies. Proposition A would require the Board of Supervisors to amend voter-approved laws to enact some of these changes. Proposition A would:
• change the language of the Charter to reflect how some City departments currently operate in order to clarify responsibilities and update rules, procedures, and reporting requirements.
• change some processes. For example: allowing legal settlements to be approved by resolution instead of by ordinance.
• require a task force to meet every ten years to recommend changes to commissions.
• eliminate or reorganize certain commissions and advisory bodies by, for example: eliminating some commissions and advisory bodies, combining and renaming some advisory bodies, and moving some commissions and advisory bodies from the Charter into the Municipal Code.
A.yes_means: If you vote “yes,” you want to amend the Charter to align it with how some City departments currently operate, change some processes, eliminate or reorganize certain commissions and advisory bodies, and require the Board of Supervisors to amend voter-approved laws to enact some of these changes.
A.no_means: If you vote “no,” you do not want to make these changes.
A.fiscal: Should the proposed Charter amendment be approved by the voters, in my opinion, it would have a moderate impact on the cost of government, saving $365,000 to $450,000 annually.
A.how_placed: On July 14, 2026, the Board of Supervisors voted 9 to 2 to place Proposition A on the ballot. The Supervisors voted as follows: Yes: Chen, Dorsey, Mahmood, Mandelman, Melgar, Sauter, Sherrill, Walton, Wong. No: Chan, Fielder.

B.title: Establishing a Municipal Finance Corporation and a Public Bank
B.question: Shall the City amend the Charter to authorize the City to establish a municipal finance corporation and a public bank?
B.way_it_is_now: A municipal finance corporation (MFC) is a government-owned non-profit corporation that makes loans but does not take deposits. A public bank is a government-owned non-profit corporation that both makes loans and takes deposits. There is no local law authorizing the City to create a municipal finance corporation or a public bank.
B.proposal:
Proposition B would amend the City Charter to authorize the City to establish a municipal finance corporation if the City has sufficient funding and resources. After three years of operation, the municipal finance corporation may become a public bank. The MFC would make loans but would not take deposits. If the MFC becomes a public bank, the public bank would make loans and also take deposits. The MFC and public bank would provide services to support:
• affordable housing development,
• affordable homeownership,
• small business development,
• environmental sustainability, and
• environmental justice. These services would be available to individual City residents and to projects and businesses located in the City. Under Proposition B, the MFC and public bank would each be governed by a board of directors. Each board would be appointed and overseen by its own oversight commission. The members of each oversight commission would be appointed by the Board of Supervisors, Mayor, Treasurer-Tax Collector, Controller, and City Attorney.
B.yes_means: If you vote “yes,” you want to authorize the City to establish a municipal finance corporation and a public bank.
B.no_means: If you vote “no,” you do not want to authorize the City to establish a municipal finance corporation and a public bank.
B.fiscal: Should the proposed Charter amendment be approved by the voters, in my opinion, it would not directly impact the cost of government as the Charter amendment does not require the City to create a Municipal Finance Corporation (MFC) that could transition into a Public Bank.
B.how_placed: On July 7, 2026, the Board of Supervisors voted 9 to 2 to place Proposition B on the ballot. The Supervisors voted as follows: Yes: Chan, Chen, Dorsey, Fielder, Mahmood, Mandelman, Melgar, Sauter, Walton. No: Sherrill, Wong.

C.title: Contributions to the Housing Trust Fund
C.question: Shall the City amend the Charter to change how the City’s annual contributions to the Housing Trust Fund are set, increase funding and expand programs for affordable housing, and extend the Fund to 2058?
C.yes_means: If you vote “yes,” you want to amend the Charter to change how the City’s annual contributions to the Housing Trust Fund are set, increase funding and expand programs for affordable housing, and extend the Fund to 2058.
C.no_means: If you vote “no,” you do not want to make these changes.
C.fiscal: Should the proposed Charter amendment be approved by the voters, in my opinion, it would have a significant impact on the cost of government of approximately $6 million in additional General Fund costs starting in Fiscal Year 2028-29, growing over time to approximately $60 million annually by Fiscal Year 2034-35.
C.how_placed: On July 14, 2026, the Board of Supervisors voted 11 to 0 to place Proposition C on the ballot. The Supervisors voted as follows: Yes: Chan, Chen, Dorsey, Fielder, Mahmood, Mandelman, Melgar, Sauter, Sherrill, Walton, Wong. No: None.

D.title: Changes to Ballot Measure Process
D.question: Shall the City amend the Charter to increase the requirements for signature initiatives from 2% to 8% of registered voters in San Francisco (currently from about 10,600 to about 42,500 signatures), increase the requirements for calling special elections, allow signature initiatives to be withdrawn before an election, and remove the ability of a minority of Board of Supervisors members or the Mayor to place measures on the ballot?
D.proposal:
Proposition D would amend the Charter to increase the requirements to put measures on the ballot by:
• Increasing the number of signatures required to place a signature initiative on the ballot from 2% to 8% (currently from about 10,600 to about 42,500 signatures) of the registered voters in San Francisco.
• Increasing the number of signatures required to call a special election on an ordinance from 10% of the votes cast for Mayor in the last election to 10% of the registered voters in San Francisco. Currently, this is about 53,100 signatures. Proposition D would allow signature initiatives to be withdrawn up to 102 days before the election. Proposition D would also change the requirements to put measures on the ballot by:
• Removing the ability of four or more Board members to place a measure on the ballot without a Board vote;
• Removing the ability of the Mayor to independently place a measure on the ballot; The Board could still place measures on the ballot by a majority vote.
D.yes_means: If you vote “yes,” you want to increase the requirements for signature initiatives from 2% to 8% of registered voters (currently from about 10,600 to about 42,500 signatures), increase the requirements for special elections, allow signature initiatives to be withdrawn, and remove the ability of a minority of Board members or the Mayor to place measures on the ballot.
D.no_means: If you vote “no,” you do not want to make these changes.
D.fiscal: Should the proposed Charter amendment be approved by the voters, in my opinion, it would have a minimal impact on the cost of government.
D.how_placed: On July 23, 2026, the Department of Elections certified that the initiative petition calling for Proposition D to be placed on the ballot had a sufficient number of valid signatures to qualify the measure for the ballot.

E.title: City Administrator’s Authority and Changes to City Contracting
E.question: Shall the City amend the Charter to give the City Administrator more authority by centralizing the City’s purchasing rules and processes, changing how the City approves purchasing rules, changing when contracts and leases require Board of Supervisors approval, and extending the City Administrator’s term?
E.way_it_is_now:
The City Administrator’s Office is responsible for most of the City’s purchasing. However, authority for the City’s purchasing and technology is shared among the City Administrator’s Office, the Board of Supervisors, the Mayor, and some City departments.
• Rules Regulating Purchasing: The Board of Supervisors (Board) may adopt ordinances that set the rules about how the City selects contractors and enters into contracts for goods, services, construction, and grants (referred to below as Purchasing).
• Board Approval of Various Agreements: With some exceptions, the City’s Charter requires the Board to approve:
• Contracts and leases that bring in $1,000,000 or more in revenue to the City, and
• Contracts that cost the City $10,000,000 or more. The Board must also approve certain amendments to these agreements.
• City Administrator’s Term: The Mayor appoints the City Administrator to a five-year term, subject to Board approval.
• City Administrator’s Authority: The City Administrator sets Purchasing rules and processes governing goods and services except for some goods and services of the Municipal Transportation Agency, Public Utilities Commission, Port Commission, and some arts departments. The City Administrator also oversees technology policies and manages disposal of City personal property for most departments.
E.proposal:
Proposition E would:
• Rules Regulating Purchasing: Give the City Administrator exclusive authority to propose ordinances that change how the City selects contractors and enters into contracts for goods, services, construction, and grants (Purchasing). The Board and Mayor may not amend the ordinances, but they can:
• Approve or reject the ordinances within 60 days, or
• If no action is taken within 60 days, the ordinances would be approved. Proposition E does not change the current Board authority for Purchasing ordinances that mainly address wages, workplace health and safety, utilization of local business, or labor agreements.
• Board Approval of Various Agreements: Increase the dollar amount requiring Board approval to:
• Contracts and leases that bring in $4,500,000 or more in revenue to the City,
• Contracts that cost the City $25,000,000 or more. Starting in 2032, the City’s Controller would adjust these dollar amounts every five years for inflation. Proposition E would require Board approval for major amendments to these agreements.
• City Administrator’s Term: Increase the City Administrator’s term from five to ten years.
• City Administrator’s Authority: The City Administrator would set Purchasing rules and processes for all goods, services, construction, and grants that all City departments must follow, except as limited by other laws. Most departments would now be subject to the City Administrator’s authority regarding technology policies and the disposal of City personal property. These rules would override those departments’ conflicting rules and policies.
E.yes_means: If you vote “yes,” you want to give the City Administrator more authority by centralizing the City’s Purchasing rules and processes, changing how the City approves Purchasing rules, changing when contracts and leases require Board approval, and extending the City Administrator’s term.
E.no_means: If you vote “no,” you do not want to make these changes.
E.fiscal: Should the proposed Charter amendment be approved by the voters, in my opinion, it would have a minimal impact on the cost of government, although at a level that cannot be determined at this time.
E.how_placed: On July 23, 2026, the Department of Elections certified that the initiative petition calling for Proposition E to be placed on the ballot had a sufficient number of valid signatures to qualify the measure for the ballot. 53,076 signatures were required to place an initiative Charter Amendment on the ballot. This number is equal to 10% of the registered voters at the time a “Notice of Intent to Circulate Petition” was published. A random check of the signatures submitted by the proponents of the initiative petition prior to the July 6, 2026, submission deadline showed that the total number of valid signatures was greater than the number required.

F.title: Changes to Executive Branch Management
F.question: Shall the City amend the Charter to expand the Mayor’s authority to transfer responsibilities between departments, hire deputy mayors, and hire some and fire most department heads; and to allow City officials to remove members of boards and commissions without cause?
F.way_it_is_now:
The Mayor is the chief executive officer of the City. The Mayor directly supervises nearly 50 City departments, which are established by Charter or ordinance. Most City departments are established by Charter.
• Transfer of Functions: The Mayor can transfer responsibilities between departments established by ordinance, as long as the Board of Supervisors (Board) does not object. The Mayor cannot transfer responsibilities for departments established by the Charter.
• Deputy Mayors: The Mayor cannot hire deputy mayors to supervise most departments established by the Charter.
• Department Heads: In most cases, the Mayor must select a department head from candidates recommended by the board or commission that oversees that department. Usually, the board or commission can fire the department head, but the Mayor cannot.
• Commissioners: In addition to the Mayor, the Board and other officials appoint members to City boards and commissions. Appointed members can usually only be suspended or removed if the member engaged in official misconduct or committed certain felonies.
F.proposal:
Proposition F would amend the Charter to allow the Mayor to do the following:
• Transfer of Functions: Transfer responsibilities between most departments or combine departments under a single department head, regardless of whether the Department was established by ordinance or Charter and as long as the Board does not object. The Mayor cannot eliminate any responsibilities established by Charter. The Mayor could also assign the oversight of these transferred responsibilities to that department’s commission. The Mayor cannot transfer responsibilities of these departments:
• City Administrator, Controller, Board of Appeals, Port, Airport, Asian Art Museum, Fine Arts Museums, San Francisco Municipal Transportation Agency, Public Utilities Commission, Civil Service Commission, Department of Human Resources, Retirement Board, Health Service System, Department of Elections, Ethics Commission, or departments headed by other elected officials. The responsibilities of the Department of Police Accountability cannot be transferred to the Police Department, and the responsibilities of the Sheriff’s Inspector General cannot be transferred to the Sheriff.
• Deputy Mayors: Hire deputy mayors to supervise most departments established by the Charter.
• Department Heads: Hire some and fire most department heads without board or commission involvement. The Mayor cannot hire or fire certain department heads that are exempt (see List of Exemptions in Words You Need To Know).
• Commissioners: In addition to the Mayor, the Board and other officials who appoint board and commission members could remove them at any time without cause. This does not apply to the Board of Appeals, Civil Service Commission, or Ethics Commission. The Mayor cannot eliminate any board or commission established by the Charter.
F.yes_means: If you vote “yes,” you want to expand the Mayor’s authority to transfer responsibilities, hire deputy mayors, hire some and fire most department heads, and allow City officials to remove members of boards or commissions without cause.
F.no_means: If you vote “no,” you do not want to make these changes.
F.fiscal: Should the proposed Charter amendment be approved by the voters, in my opinion, it would have a minimal impact on the cost of government, although at a level that cannot be determined at this time.
F.how_placed: On July 23, 2026, the Department of Elections certified that the initiative petition calling for Proposition F to be placed on the ballot had a sufficient number of valid signatures to qualify the measure for the ballot. 53,076 signatures were required to place an initiative Charter Amendment on the ballot. This number is equal to 10% of the registered voters at the time a “Notice of Intent to Circulate Petition” was published. A random check of the signatures submitted by the proponents of the initiative petition prior to the July 6, 2026, submission deadline showed that the total number of valid signatures was greater than the number required.

G.title: Allowing Private Vehicles on the Upper Great Highway in Sunset Dunes Park
G.question: Shall the City close Sunset Dunes Park from Monday at 4:00 a.m. through Friday at 6:00 p.m., unless a holiday falls on a weekday, in order to reopen the roadway known as the Upper Great Highway to private vehicles during that time?
G.way_it_is_now: Sunset Dunes Park is an open recreational space that replaced the Great Highway between Lincoln Way and Sloat Boulevard (Upper Great Highway) and is closed to private vehicles at all times. Sunset Dunes Park (former Upper Great Highway) is open to emergency vehicles, official government vehicles, intra-park transit shuttle buses, and similar authorized vehicles.
G.proposal: Proposition G would close Sunset Dunes Park from Monday at 4:00 a.m. through Friday at 6:00 p.m., unless a holiday falls on a weekday, in order to reopen the roadway known as the Upper Great Highway to private vehicles during that time. The Upper Great Highway will remain open to emergency vehicles, official government vehicles, intra-park transit shuttle buses, and similar authorized vehicles. Proposition G would require the City to obtain all necessary approvals, including any permits required by the California Coastal Act or from other government agencies, to reopen the roadway known as the Upper Great Highway to private vehicles.
G.yes_means: If you vote “yes,” you want to close Sunset Dunes Park from Monday at 4:00 a.m. through Friday at 6:00 p.m., unless a holiday falls on a weekday, in order to reopen the roadway known as the Upper Great Highway to private vehicles during that time.
G.no_means: If you vote “no,” you do not want the City to make these changes.
G.fiscal: Should the proposed Ordinance be approved by the voters and the roadway is open to private vehicles, in my opinion, it would significantly increase the cost of government by approximately $9.8 million in one-time capital costs and by approximately $500,000 to $1.9 million annually.
G.how_placed: On July 23, 2026, the Department of Elections certified that the initiative petition calling for Proposition G to be placed on the ballot had a sufficient number of valid signatures to qualify the measure for the ballot. 10,615 signatures were required to place an initiative ordinance on the ballot. This number is equal to 2% of the registered voters at the time a “Notice of Intent to Circulate Petition” was published. A random check of the signatures submitted by the proponents of the initiative petition prior to the July 6, 2026, submission deadline showed that the total number of valid signatures was greater than the number required.

H.title: Parcel Tax to Fund Muni Operations
H.question: Shall the City fund Muni service through a new annual parcel tax on real estate at rates ranging from $129 per parcel up to a maximum of $400,000 per parcel, depending on the type of property and its size and adjusted annually for inflation, for estimated revenue of $177 million a year for 15 years?
H.way_it_is_now: The Municipal Railway (Muni) provides public transit in San Francisco, including bus, light rail, streetcar, and cable car. Muni provides over 500,000 rides per weekday. Muni service is funded by transit fares and local, state and federal sources, but not through a parcel tax. State law limits the total revenue, including tax revenue, that the City may spend each year. The voters may approve increases to this limit for up to four years. Owners of rent-controlled residential property in the City are generally limited in what costs they can pass onto their tenants.
H.proposal:
Starting July 1, 2027, and continuing until June 30, 2042, Proposition H would fund Muni service through a new annual parcel tax on real estate in San Francisco. The tax would be adjusted annually for inflation. The proposed 2027 tax rates would be:
• Single-Family Residential Parcels:
• A base tax of $129.
• For buildings with more than 3,000 square feet of building area:
• $0.42 per square foot between 3,001 and 5,000, and
• $1.99 per square foot over 5,000.
• Multifamily Residential Parcels:
• A base tax of $249.
• For buildings with more than 5,000 square feet of building area:
• $0.195 per square foot over 5,000.
• This tax is capped at $50,000 per parcel.
• Non-Residential Parcels:
• A base tax of $799.
• For buildings with more than 5,000 square feet of building area:
• $0.76 per square foot between 5,001 and 50,000,
• $0.84 per square foot between 50,001 and 250,000, and
• $0.99 per square foot over 250,000.
• This tax is capped at $400,000 per parcel.
• Mixed-Use Parcels:
• A base tax of $799.
• For buildings with more than 5,000 square feet of building area:
• A combination of the marginal rates for residential and non-residential parcels above.
• This tax is capped at $400,000 per parcel.
• Parcels with No Buildings:
• No base tax.
• $392 for land area over 2,000 square feet. The tax would not apply to: 1. Properties or portions of properties not required to pay standard property taxes; and 2. Single Room Occupancy (SRO) units and their shared facilities such as kitchens or bathrooms. Most homeowners aged 65 or older living in their primary home would get a discount or pay no tax. Revenues from the tax would only be used for Muni service and administering the tax. In addition to the annual required audit by an independent auditor, an annual report and efficiency review would be required. This measure would increase the City’s spending limit for four years. Owners could pass up to 50% of the tax onto tenants in rent-controlled units where the rent was set before June 1, 2027, up to a maximum of $65 per unit per year.
H.yes_means: If you vote “yes,” you want the City to fund Muni service through a new annual parcel tax on real estate.
H.no_means: If you vote “no,” you do not want to make these changes.
H.fiscal: Should the proposed parcel tax be approved by the voters, in my opinion, based on currently available parcel data it would generate approximately $177 million annually for Muni transit service starting in Fiscal Year (FY) 2027-2028, and would increase over time as the per parcel taxes are adjusted for inflation each year.
H.how_placed: On June 12, 2026, the Department of Elections certified that the initiative petition calling for Proposition H to be placed on the ballot had a sufficient number of valid signatures to qualify the measure for the ballot. 10,615 signatures were required to place an initiative ordinance on the ballot. This number is equal to 2% of the registered voters at the time a “Notice of Intent to Circulate Petition” was published. A random check of the signatures submitted by the proponents of the initiative petition prior to the July 6, 2026, submission deadline showed that the total number of valid signatures was greater than the number required.

I.title: Changes to Real Property Transfer Tax
I.question: Shall the City permanently dedicate half of the transfer tax revenues collected when certain real estate with a value or sales price of more than $10,000,000 changes hands, which will continue to be taxed at rates of 5.5% to 6%, to be spent only on affordable housing, including social housing developments and housing assistance, and exempt certain sales from the dedicated portion of the tax, for an estimated annual revenue decrease of approximately $1 million?
I.way_it_is_now:
The City collects a transfer tax when most real estate changes hands. The tax rates depend on the property’s sales price or value and the two highest tax rates are:
• 5.5% for properties between $10,000,000 and under $25,000,000, and
• 6% for properties at $25,000,000 or more. Some real estate transfers are exempt from the tax or are subject to reduced rates.
• Reduce the transfer tax from 6% to 3%
• Impose a new transfer tax of 3% This measure will not increase the tax rate on the transfer of any property above what is charged today. The same exemptions and tax reductions from the current transfer tax would still apply to the new transfer tax. The new transfer tax would also exempt the first sale of certain multifamily real estate if it is sold within 5 years of completion of new residential units. Tax Revenue Spending Revenues generated from the transfer tax may be spent for any governmental purpose. The City could spend revenue from the new transfer tax only on: The Board of Supervisors (Board) may amend, reduce, suspend, or repeal the transfer tax without voter approval. Voters must approve any increase of the transfer tax. State law limits the total revenue, including tax revenue, the City may spend each year. The voters may approve increases to this limit for up to four years.
I.proposal:
Proposition I would dedicate half of the transfer tax revenues when certain real estate with a value or sales price of more than $10,000,000 changes hands, to be spent only on affordable housing, including social housing developments and housing assistance. Specifically, the measure would: Transfer Tax For properties with a sales price or value between $10,000,000 and under $25,000,000:
• Reduce the current transfer tax from 5.5% to 2.75%
• Impose a new transfer tax of 2.75% For properties with a sales price or value at $25,000,000 or more:
• At least 60% for affordable housing production, with at least half to social housing developments;
• At least 25% towards the acquisition or rehabilitation of affordable housing, with at least 60% to acquisition of existing housing units; and
• At least 10% to tenant stabilization/homeless prevention programs, with at least half to eviction defense and prevention; The Board could only change the transfer tax consistent with the purpose of the tax. All other changes would require voter approval. Proposition I would approve an unlimited number of new affordable housing units for low-income households funded by revenue from the new transfer tax. Proposition I would require the City to submit annual reports to the Board and Mayor on the use of the new tax revenue. Proposition I would increase the City’s spending limit for four years.
I.yes_means: If you vote “yes,” you want to dedicate half of the transfer tax revenues when certain real estate with a value or sales price of more than $10,000,000 changes hands, to be spent only on affordable housing, including social housing developments and housing assistance.
I.no_means: If you vote “no,” you do not want to make these changes.
I.fiscal: Should the proposed ordinance be approved by the voters, in my opinion, it would represent a moderate annual decrease of approximately $1 million to the City’s overall revenues starting in Fiscal Year (FY) 2027-28.
I.how_placed: On July 23, 2026, the Department of Elections certified that the initiative petition calling for Proposition I to be placed on the ballot had a sufficient number of valid signatures to qualify the measure for the ballot. 10,644 signatures were required to place an initiative ordinance on the ballot. This number is equal to 2% of the registered voters at the time a “Notice of Intent to Circulate Petition” was published. A random check of the signatures submitted by the proponents of the initiative petition prior to the July 6, 2026, submission deadline showed that the total number of valid signatures was greater than the number required.

J.title: Removal of Foreclosure Exemption for Real Property Transfer Tax
J.question: Shall the City permanently apply a transfer tax of between 0.5% and 6% of a property’s fair market value, on the transfer of properties such as commercial, industrial, and large residential properties, that are transferred to a lender because of foreclosure or to avoid foreclosure, for estimated annual revenue of $100 million to $150 million?
J.way_it_is_now: San Francisco charges a tax when most real estate property in the City changes hands. The amount of the tax depends on the property’s sales price or value. When a lender takes over a property through foreclosure, or when an owner hands over a property to the lender to avoid foreclosure, there is a tax break. The lender pays tax only on the difference between what the property sold for and what is still owed to the lender, including interest and foreclosure costs. State law limits the total revenue, including tax revenue, the City may spend each year. The voters may approve increases to this limit for up to four years.
J.proposal: Proposition J would apply a transfer tax for properties such as commercial, industrial, and large residential real estate that a lender takes through foreclosure or is handed over to the lender to avoid foreclosure. Starting March 1, 2027, these properties would be taxed on their full market value. The tax break would still apply to the transfer of: 1. single-family residences, 2. multi-family residential buildings with fewer than five units, and 3. mixed-use properties with fewer than five residential units and only one floor of non-residential space. Proposition J would increase the City’s spending limit for four years.
J.yes_means: If you vote “yes,” you want to apply a transfer tax for properties such as commercial, industrial, and large residential properties, that are transferred to a lender because of foreclosure.
J.no_means: If you vote “no,” you do not want to make these changes.
J.fiscal: Should the proposed initiative ordinance be approved by the voters, in my opinion, it would significantly increase the City’s Real Property Transfer Tax revenues although the amount generated each year would be unpredictable and likely to change significantly year-to-year.
J.how_placed: On July 28, 2026, the Board of Supervisors voted 10 to 0, with one Supervisor excused, to place Proposition J on the ballot. The Supervisors voted as follows: Yes: Chan, Chen, Dorsey, Fielder, Mahmood, Mandelman, Melgar, Sauter, Sherrill, Wong. No: None. Excused: Walton.
